label: ACL rule order and first match wins

mentor.diagnosis: You wrote rules that are individually correct but in an order that makes some of them unreachable. An ACL is evaluated top to bottom and stops at the first match.
contrast: Below a broad rule that already matched
Placed before the permit for its subnet
Placed after, so it never runs
mentor.rule: Specific before general, always. If a broader rule above already matches the traffic, everything below it for that traffic is dead code.
mentor.tell: Any task mixing a subnet wide permit with a single host deny is testing ordering. Put the exception first.
mentor.trap: The rule set looks complete because every required line is present. Graders simulate the traffic, so a shadowed rule scores as if you never wrote it.

label: The implicit deny at the end of an ACL

mentor.diagnosis: You either added an explicit permit any at the end, or you assumed traffic not mentioned would be allowed. Firewalls deny by default.
contrast: Yes, at the bottom of every ACL
Yes, which is why you add it
Adding permit any at the end
mentor.rule: Anything you did not explicitly permit is already denied. Write an explicit deny any at the bottom only to get logging, never a permit any.
mentor.tell: 'Deny all other traffic' in the requirements usually needs no rule at all. It is already true. Check whether the task wants it logged.
mentor.trap: 'Deny all other traffic' reads like an instruction to add a rule, and adding an explicit deny any is harmless. Adding permit any is the failure, and it is the option that makes the other requirements appear to pass.

label: Source vs destination, and which side holds the well known port

mentor.diagnosis: You put the service port on the wrong side of the rule, or reversed source and destination. The server listens on the well known port, the client uses a random high port.
contrast: Your host, on an ephemeral port
mentor.rule: The destination port is the service. The source port is almost always any. Write the rule in the direction the connection is initiated.
mentor.tell: 'Allow the internet to reach the web server' means destination is the server and destination port is 443. Never source port 443.
mentor.trap: Source port 443 looks symmetric and tidy. It matches only the return traffic, which a stateful firewall already handles.

label: Using any where the requirement named a specific host or port

mentor.diagnosis: Your rule permits the required traffic, but also a great deal more. Passing the functional test is not the same as passing least privilege.
contrast: Exactly the host, port and direction required
any, or a whole subnet, or all ports
Partial credit at best, often zero for that subtask
mentor.rule: Use any only where the requirement genuinely says any, which is usually only the source of inbound internet traffic.
mentor.tell: If the scenario names a specific management workstation, the source must be that host's address, not its subnet and not any.
mentor.trap: The traffic test passes, so the rule feels correct. Graders check breadth as well as function, exactly as a real auditor would.

label: Writing return traffic rules on a stateful firewall

mentor.diagnosis: You added a second rule to allow the replies. A stateful firewall tracks the connection and permits the return automatically.
contrast: In the context of its connection
mentor.rule: On a stateful firewall write one rule per connection, in the direction it is initiated. The reply is free.
mentor.tell: If the question describes a modern firewall or NGFW, do not write reverse rules. If it says stateless packet filter or classic router ACL, you must.
mentor.trap: Adding the return rule seems safely thorough. On a stateful device it is an unnecessary opening and usually scores as an overbroad rule.

label: What a screened subnet (DMZ) is allowed to initiate

mentor.diagnosis: You allowed the DMZ host to open connections into the internal LAN. The entire point of the zone is that a compromised DMZ host cannot reach inside.
contrast: That is what the DMZ is for
No, except one named flow if required
A compromised public host must not pivot inward
Inside is more trusted than outside
No direct path from untrusted to trusted
mentor.rule: Trust flows inward to outward. The DMZ may be reached from the internet and from inside, but it initiates nothing into the internal network unless a requirement explicitly names that one flow.
mentor.tell: 'The web server must query the internal database' is that explicit exception. Permit exactly that one host, one port, nothing more.
mentor.trap: The application genuinely needs the database, so a broad DMZ to LAN permit makes the app work. It also hands an attacker the pivot the design exists to prevent.

mentor.diagnosis: You picked a general purpose firewall for an application specific attack, or the reverse.
contrast: One box, one licence, all features
mentor.rule: Attack against the application logic means WAF. Broad perimeter control with application and user awareness means NGFW. One appliance doing everything for a small site means UTM.
mentor.tell: The words SQL injection, cross site scripting, or OWASP in the stem point to a WAF.
mentor.trap: An NGFW is more capable overall, so it reads like the stronger answer. For a targeted web application attack the specialised device is the correct one.

label: IDS vs IPS, and inline vs tap placement

mentor.diagnosis: You chose a device that can only watch when the requirement was to stop the traffic, or you placed a blocking device out of the traffic path.
contrast: Tap or SPAN port, out of band
Sees a copy or the real packets
The network may stop, so fail mode matters
mentor.rule: To stop an attack the device must be inline, which makes it an IPS. If it is out of band it can only tell you afterwards.
mentor.tell: 'Prevent', 'block', 'stop in real time' means IPS. 'Alert', 'detect', 'no impact on traffic flow' means IDS.
mentor.trap: An IDS is safer to deploy and tuning is less risky, which makes it attractive. It cannot satisfy a requirement that uses the word prevent.

mentor.diagnosis: You credited NAT with security it does not provide. Hiding addresses is a side effect, not a policy.
contrast: Yes, if you tell it to
Inbound connections have nowhere to land by default
mentor.rule: NAT is not a security control. It makes unsolicited inbound connections awkward, which is not the same as denying them by policy.
mentor.tell: Any option that answers a filtering requirement with 'enable NAT' is a distractor.
mentor.trap: It is true that NAT makes inbound access harder, so the option contains a half truth. The exam wants the control that enforces the stated policy.
